L.t: Your first month in a kitchen
L.k: Learn in this order: rules and safety, then proteins, sauces, dough, service, and cost.
p: Day 1: kitchen rules, food safety, knife skills, allergens, glossary.
Day 2: allergen quiz on your menu.
Week 1: meat and protein, fish and seafood.
Week 2: sauces and stocks, starch and dough.
Week 3: buffet, service flow, plating, breakfast station.
Month 1: food cost, waste, quality control.
Ask the chef to sign off each block when you can explain it at the station.

L.k: Product, consistency, precision, identity, balance. Every plate matches the recipe card and the photo.
p: Few ingredients, each with a purpose; local and seasonal.
Balance salt, acid, fat, heat, sweet, bitter, umami; contrast texture and temperature.
One hero plus 3–5 edible elements; odd numbers, negative space, clean rims.
Hot plates 60–65 °C, cold plates 2–4 °C. Same direction on every plate.
Tasting menu: light to rich, cold to hot, acid to fat; no main ingredient twice; always a vegetarian version.
Tasting course every 12–18 min; the whole table served together.
x: Garnish that adds nothing to flavour.
Sauce drowning the plate.

L.k: One voice calls the orders. Answer "Yes, chef" so the caller knows you heard.
p: Order in → Fire → Pick up. "All day" is the total of one item on open tickets.
Call "Behind", "Hot", "Sharp", "Corner" when moving.
"86" means the item is finished.
Daily briefing: covers, VIPs, allergies, menu changes, 86 items, specials.
Open the Glossary tool for 150+ terms in English, Bulgarian and Russian.

r: Runs a section: garde manger, sauce, fish, grill, pastry

x: Silent cooks: the pass never knows who heard.

L.k: A sharp knife, a fixed board and the claw grip. A falling knife is never caught.
p: Damp cloth under the board so it cannot slide.
Claw grip: fingertips tucked, knuckles guide the blade.
Never leave knives in the sink or under a cloth. Carry point down, blade back, say "knife" behind people.
Hone before each shift; sharpen when honing no longer helps. A dull knife slips.
Purple board and separate tools for allergen-free orders.
x: Catching a falling knife.
Raw chicken on the green board.
Knife hidden in a sink full of water.

L.k: Same size means same cooking time. A tray of mixed sizes is redone.
p: Square off the vegetable first so it sits flat.
Cut planks, then sticks, then dice.
Mirepoix ratio: onion 2 : carrot 1 : celery 1.
Trimmings go to stock where possible.
x: Uneven dice: half burnt, half raw.
Ordering on net weight, forgetting the trim.

L.k: Long jobs first, herbs last, everything labelled, tasted and checked 30 min before service.
p: Read the menu, prep list and covers.
Check the fridge: leftovers, use-by dates, labels. First expiring, first used (FIFO).
Write the prep list with quantities from par levels.
Prep order: stocks, braises, doughs, then sauces, then vegetables, herbs last.
Set the station: boards, knives, cloths, sanitiser, tasting spoons, warm or chilled plates.
Label every container: product, date, use-by, initials.
Taste every sauce and garnish.

r: Leftovers labelled, cooled, stored or binned
Boards and knives washed, sanitised, dried
Allergen board and recipe cards at hand
Station wiped, floor clean, bins emptied

x: Unlabelled containers.
Herbs chopped at 8 am for dinner.
No tasting before service.

L.t: Five rules to know by heart
L.k: Cold 0–4 °C, hot 63 °C +, cool to 10 °C in 2 h, reheat 75 °C once, label everything.
p: Fridge 0–4 °C, freezer −18 °C or colder. Record twice per shift.
Hot holding 63 °C or above.
Cool cooked food from 63 °C to below 10 °C within 2 hours (blast chiller).
Reheat to 75 °C core, once only.
Every container: product, date made, use-by, initials. No label, no use.
First expiring, first out (FEFO) for fresh and high-risk food.
x: Cooling a full stockpot on the bench.
Reheating a sauce twice.

L.k: Never guess. Check the recipe card and the label of every bought-in product.
p: Chefsheet numbers allergens 1–14 as below; check which order your own menus use.
Fish (4), crustaceans (2) and molluscs (12) are three separate allergens. Never write "seafood".

Hidden sources: anchovy in Caesar and Worcestershire, soy lecithin in chocolate, sulphites in wine and dried fruit, mustard in sausages, sesame on pastries, milk in mash and scrambled eggs, gluten in sausages and stock cubes.
"May contain" counts as contains for an allergy order.
Read labels at every new delivery and every new supplier.

r: Soy sauce, stock cubes, beer, breadcrumbs
Wine, dried fruit, some frozen shrimp

x: Writing "shellfish" on the menu.
Answering a guest from memory.

L.k: One cook makes an allergy order from start to finish, with clean tools; a mistake means start again.
p: Ticket says ALLERGY and the allergen; the chef is told in person.
Check the recipe card and every label. Unclear means not served.
Washed hands, purple board, clean knife and pan, fresh oil or oven.
No garnish, sauce or oil from the shared line.
Tag the plate and carry it separately.
Treat every request as an allergy unless the guest clearly says intolerance.
Anaphylaxis: swelling of lips or throat, breathing trouble, collapse. Call 112, tell the manager, help with their adrenaline pen, keep plate and packaging.

r: Meat or fish stock, gelatine, anchovy, lard, animal rennet in Parmesan
Vegetable stock, agar, vegetarian hard cheese
Butter in rice, egg pasta, brioche, mayo, egg wash, honey
Olive oil, durum pasta, plant cream, aquafaba
Soy sauce, stock cubes, flour on the board, beer, shared fryer, pasta water
Tamari, GF pasta in fresh water, polenta, rice
Every dairy product incl. butter, whey, casein
Treat as vegan for dairy; lactose-free is NOT safe
Lard, ham, pork gelatine, cured sausages
Stock with vinegar or lemon; alcohol does not fully cook off

x: Lactose-free milk for a milk allergy.
Fries from the shared fryer for a coeliac.

A guest with a milk allergy can have lactose-free milk.
A label says "may contain nuts". For a nut-allergy order you:

L.k: Use the probe, pull 3–5 °C below target and rest. Touch is a check, not the measure.
p: Heat the grill 15 min and brush the bars hot. Set a hot zone to sear and a cooler zone to finish.
Whole cuts out of the fridge 20–30 min before; never minced meat or poultry. Pat dry.
Oil the meat, not the grill. Do not move it for 2 min, turn 45° for cross marks, flip once (thin cuts).
Probe side-on into the thickest part. Check the probe in iced water: 0 °C ± 1.
Rest on a rack or board, not in its juices. Slice against the grain.
x: Grill not hot enough: grey meat, no crust, sticking.
Pressing with the spatula: juices lost.
Cutting to check doneness instead of probing.
Same tongs for raw and cooked meat.
Skipping the rest.

L.k: Whole beef and lamb may be pink; minced meat, poultry and anything reheated may not.
p: Bacteria sit on the surface of a whole muscle, and the sear kills them. Mincing moves the surface inside.
A guest asking for a pink burger gets a polite no.
Reheat once only, to 75 °C core.
Cool cooked meat from 63 °C to below 10 °C within 2 hours, label, chill at 0–4 °C.
Raw meat is stored covered, on the bottom shelf.
x: Trusting colour instead of the probe.
Reheating a batch twice.
Cooling cooked meat slowly at room temperature.

L.k: Above 40 °C proteins tighten and push water out. Temperature and time together decide juiciness.
p: Chicken breast at 74 °C is safe but dry. Pre-salted and held at 65 °C long enough it is safe and juicy.
Salt at 1 % of meat weight raises water holding by up to 15 %. Leave 1–24 h; do not rinse.
Acid denatures protein without heat (ceviche). Over 60 min in lemon, vinegar or wine, fillets turn mealy.
Match the method to collagen, not price: tender cuts low and short, tough cuts long braise.
Collagen turns to gelatine at 70–80 °C over time. Acid does not tenderise ribs or brisket; time does.

r: Flaky and moist: the service window

x: The crust 'seals in juices': it does not, it makes flavour.
Salting only when the meat is already in the pan for thick cuts that could have been dry-brined.
Marinating fish in citrus for hours.

L.k: Egg texture is set by temperature, not by time. 63–65 °C gives a soft gel.
p: White starts to set at 62 °C and is firm at 80 °C; yolk sets at 65–70 °C.
63–65 °C for 45–60 min gives an onsen egg with a soft, half-liquid centre.
The grey-green ring is iron sulphide from overcooking. Cook less and chill immediately.
For stable meringue add acid (lemon, cream of tartar) and sugar gradually; skip salt.
Yolk emulsifies (lecithin), white does not. Mayonnaise needs yolk.
Pasteurise eggs at 57 °C for 1–2 h for tartare, mayonnaise and raw desserts.
x: Boiling at 100 °C for soft eggs: rubbery white.
Leaving boiled eggs in hot water.
Using unpasteurised eggs for raw sauces on a buffet.

L.k: Brining modifies the protein so it loses less water when cooked. Dry brine is the default for quality.
p: Salt first draws surface moisture out, then diffusion carries salt and water back in. The return takes time.
Dry brine: salt only, uncovered on a rack, best crust and flavour. Errors cannot be fixed.
Wet brine: 3–6 % salt in water (30–60 g per litre). Forgiving, good for lean poultry, weaker browning.
Sugar in a brine max 50 % of the salt, or it burns on the sear.
Always at 0–4 °C, product fully covered, food-grade containers.
Correct brining returns 5–8 % more yield.
x: Measuring salt by spoon instead of weight.
Wet brine too long: ham texture, irreversible.
Not drying before cooking.
Brine plus an aggressive acid marinade.

L.t: Salt tables: dry salting & quick brines
L.k: Product weight × salt % ÷ 100 = grams of salt. Weigh it.
p: Example: 1,200 g pork neck at 1.3 % = 15.6 g salt.
Seafood counts in minutes, poultry in hours.
Minced meat is salted right before cooking.
Brine percentages are salt in water, not on the product.
Dry after brining, add no extra salt, add acid after cooking.
x: Iodised table salt for brines.
Fine salt at coarse-salt quantities: over-salted.
Salting fish for an hour.

L.k: Salt 12–24 h ahead, or right before cooking. Never 5–30 min before.
p: Dry brine 12–24 h: total loss 11–13 %, best crust.
Salting just before beats no salt: 15–18 % loss vs 18–22 %.
Salting and waiting 5–30 min gives the worst texture: water is out and not back.
The gap between best and worst is about 9 points of yield, over 20 g on a 250 g steak.
x: Salting steaks at the start of service and cooking them 20 min later.

L.k: Bath temperature is the target core temperature. Time sets uniformity and safety.
p: Salt goes in before vacuum sealing.
The sear adds 1–2 °C; with a hard sear choose the lower end of the range.
After the bath: dry completely, sear 30–45 s per side.
Below 60 °C, poultry and pork need a pasteurisation hold: follow a time–temperature table, never guess.
Do not hold proteins indefinitely at target; chill fast if not going to service.
x: Wet surface at the sear.
Salting after the bath.
Holding fish for hours at bath temperature.

L.k: The method changes yield more than the product. Price the grill accordingly.
p: Sous-vide gives the highest yield on every product; grilling the lowest.
Lean cuts lose most: lamb leg, striploin, pork loin.
Plan backwards: raw = cooked portion ÷ yield. 180 g grilled striploin at 72 % = 250 g raw.
These are reference figures. Weigh your own product before costing.
x: Sizing portions on raw weight.
Using one yield figure for every method.

L.k: Dry surface, hot stable pan, full contact, thin fat layer. Miss one and you get grey meat.
p: Maillard browning needs a dry surface at 140–165 °C; sugars caramelise at 160–180 °C and turn bitter above.
Cast iron for thick steaks, carbon steel for controlled sears, stainless for pan sauces, plancha for many portions.
Thin cuts: flip once. Thick steaks: turn often for an even gradient. Skin-on fish: barely move it.
Never overcrowd: steam builds and the crust is gone.
Carry-over: boneless steak +3–5 °C, bone-in +5–7 °C. Pull early.
x: Cold pan.
Crowding the pan.
Butter from the start at high heat.

Minced meat burgers are cooked to:
Worst time to salt a steak before cooking:

Which method gives the highest yield?

L.k: Fresh fish arrives at 0–2 °C on ice and is used within 48 hours.
p: Keep shellfish harvest tags for 60 days.
Fresh fish: perforated tray over crushed ice, covered, bottom shelf, 0–2 °C. Drain melt water daily.
Live molluscs: damp cloth, 2–4 °C, never in water or a sealed bag.
Ready-to-eat seafood always above raw fish.
Opened smoked salmon: 3 days, labelled.
Thaw in the fridge 12–24 h, or sealed under cold running water. Never refreeze.

r: Sunken eyes, grey gills, soft flesh, ammonia smell
Frost inside the bag, freezer burn
Cracked shells, open shells that do not close

x: Thawing on the bench.
Mussels stored in water.

L.k: Wild fish served raw or below 60 °C is frozen first to −20 °C core for 24 h.
p: Applies to tartare, ceviche, gravlax and pink salmon (EU Reg. 853/2004).
Record the freezing date on the label.
Tuna, mackerel and sardines form histamine above 4 °C. Cooking does not destroy it.
Reject any of them delivered above 4 °C.
x: Fresh wild salmon served pink without freezing.
Tuna left on the pass.

L.k: Blue board only, weigh your own yields monthly and use them in gross weights.
p: Round fish: scale, gut, cut behind the head, fillet along the backbone, pin-bone against the grain.
Salmon side: trim belly fat and bloodline, pin-bone, portion 160–180 g net.
Shrimp: peel, cut the back, remove the vein, dry well. 16/20 = 16–20 pieces per 454 g.
Mussels: scrub, pull the beard towards the hinge just before cooking.
x: Buying net weight for a gross-weight recipe.

L.k: Fish tolerates less heat than meat: pull at 48–50 °C, serve at 50–55 °C, or 63 °C fully cooked.
p: Skin-on: dry the skin, hot pan, skin side 80 % of the time, press 10 s to keep it flat.
Shrimp: very hot pan, single layer, 1–2 min per side. C-shape is done, O-shape is overcooked.
Poach at 70–80 °C, never boiling.
Mussels: lid on, high heat 3–5 min; discard any that stay closed.
Fish, crustaceans and molluscs are three separate allergens (4, 2, 12). Never write "seafood".
x: Boiling poached fish.
Crowding shrimp: they stew.

quiz: Wild salmon served pink must first be frozen to:
Histamine in tuna is destroyed by cooking.
Shrimp is overcooked when it is:

L.k: Start cold, never boil, skim early, salt only at the end.
p: Boiling emulsifies fat and clouds the stock; it cannot be undone.
Temperature control overrides time.
Roast bones and mirepoix for brown stocks.
Fish stock is fragile: 20–40 min only.
x: Salting stock before reduction.
Hard boil to save time.

L.k: Body comes from gelatine, not flour. Season at the end: reduction concentrates salt.
p: Reduce at a medium heat: high burns aromas, low is too slow.
Water evaporates, salt stays. Salt the base lightly.
The sauce coats the protein; it does not pool.
Mount cold butter off the heat for shine; it breaks above 70 °C.
Final salt and acid are the last adjustment before the pass.
x: Salting at the start of a reduction.
Thickening with flour to fake body.

L.k: 1 part roux to 10 parts liquid. Warm liquid into the roux, or you get lumps.
p: Mirepoix builds aroma through browning and natural sugars.
Roux: equal flour and butter, cooked to remove the raw taste. White for béchamel, dark for meat and mushroom sauces.
Do not boil béchamel hard: starch breaks and the sauce thins.
Strain every sauce before service.
Starch slurry gives a clearer sauce; roux a richer, heavier one.
x: Too much flour: pasty, gluey sauce.
Diluting a thick sauce with water instead of stock.

L.k: Fat + water + emulsifier + mechanical energy. Remove one and it fails.
p: Cold emulsions (mayonnaise, vinaigrette) are low risk; hot ones (hollandaise, béarnaise) very high.
Work hot emulsions at 55–65 °C: below 55 °C fat separates, above 65 °C egg coagulates.
Mayonnaise ingredients at 18–22 °C; cold oil breaks it.
Add fat slowly; acid for structure early, acid for taste late.
Never hold emulsions on direct heat: bain-marie or very low heat.

r: Restart on a fresh yolk, add broken sauce slowly
Whisk, add a little warm water
Breaks with acid plus high heat

x: Reheating hollandaise or mayonnaise.
Thickening a broken sauce to hide it.

L.k: A flat dish usually lacks acid, not salt. Add acid, then taste before the second salting.
p: Acid cuts fat and refreshes the palate: lemon on duck, vinegar in a pork ragout.
Acid makes salt taste stronger. With tomato, wine or vinegar, salt goes in last.
Too sweet: add acid, not salt. Too fatty: acid or a bitter element. Too salty: acid and sweetness together; water and potatoes do not remove salt.
Below pH 4.6 milk and egg proteins curdle. Lemon into hot cream splits it: cool first, dilute, or use full-fat cream.
Acid goes in at the end; long cooking drives off citrus aromas.
x: Fixing a flat sauce with more salt.
Lemon straight into boiling cream.

L.k: Pasta and sauce finish together in the pan; starchy pasta water is the emulsifier.
p: The sauce should come together in 30–60 seconds; longer means a mistake earlier.
Never boil after cream or egg goes in.
Seafood: pasta goes into the sauce, never the reverse.
Cheese sauces (cacio e pepe): heat control plus starch stop splitting.
x: Sauce poured over plated pasta.
Draining all the pasta water.

quiz: A broken mayonnaise is fixed by:
Whisking it slowly into a fresh yolk
When do you salt a reduction?
A sauce tastes flat. Usually it lacks:
Seafood pasta: which goes into which?

L.k: Green vegetables: short boil in plenty of salted water, then straight into iced water.
p: Long cooking in acid turns chlorophyll olive-brown.
A little vinegar keeps beetroot and red cabbage red.
Acid keeps pectin firm: peas in tomato sauce take longer. Add acid to greens late.
Baking soda softens fast but destroys texture, vitamin C and taste. Neon green usually means soda.
Blanch 2–3 min and shock in ice to stop the enzymes.
Slow-cooked onions and garlic turn sweet as sulphur compounds break down.
x: Lid on while boiling greens.
Throwing away the cooking water: it goes to soups and sauces.

L.k: Starch thickens at 70–80 °C. Maillard needs protein and a dry surface above 140 °C; caramel needs sugar above 160 °C.
p: Over-stirring or over-boiling bursts starch granules and the sauce thins again.
Fat carries aromas that water cannot extract.
Butter smokes around 200 °C, refined oils above 230 °C.
Caramel is chemically changed sugar, not melted sugar.
x: Browning wet meat.
Boiling a cornflour sauce for 20 min.

L.k: Warm stock in portions, steady stirring, mantecatura off the heat, serve at once all'onda.
p: Use Arborio, Carnaroli or Vialone Nano; never wash the rice.
Stock at 70–80 °C; cold stock stops the starch release.
Sweat the onion clear, not brown. Wine about 10 % of the total liquid.
Stir rhythmically, not aggressively.
Off the heat: cold butter and low-moisture hard cheese. No cream needed.
Mushrooms, seafood and vegetables go in at the end. Lightly salted stock: rice absorbs salt.
x: All the stock at once: boiled rice.
Holding risotto 10 min: it turns gluey.

L.k: Hydration decides how dough behaves, time decides how strong it gets. Resting is not optional.
p: Water as % of flour. Salt 2 %, fresh yeast 1–3 %, dry yeast one third of fresh.
Dough after kneading 24–26 °C.
Windowpane test: a piece stretches thin without tearing.
Proofed when a finger dent springs back slowly.
Overmixing tightens the dough; gnocchi turn gluey.
x: Skipping the rest.
Warm water in summer: over-proofed dough.

L.k: Pastry is chemistry: weigh to the gram, small amounts on a 0.1 g scale.
p: Cold butter for pastry, room temperature for cakes.
Preheat the oven 15 min; check with an oven thermometer.
Raw-egg desserts (mousse, tiramisu): pasteurised eggs only.
Nut desserts use separate tools and are plated last.

r: Dry the panade, eggs one by one
Soak cold, add to warm, not boiling
Boil 1 min, sets at ~40 °C, holds warm
Rest 30 min before and after rolling
Blind bake, egg wash, 3 min more
Bake dry, keep oven shut 15 min

x: Cups and spoons instead of grams.
Gelatine into boiling liquid.

quiz: Boiled briefly in salted water and shocked in ice

L.k: Under the brine, no oxygen, non-iodised salt, 18–22 °C, and a measured pH.
p: Lactobacilli turn sugars into lactic acid; pH below 4.6 stops pathogens.
Vegetables 1.5–2.5 % salt (2 % on cabbage); dairy 0.7–1 %. Above 5 % stops the good cultures.
Iodised salt and detergent residue kill the culture.
Stop fermentation by chilling to 4 °C.
Yoghurt thickens as casein bonds near pH 4.6; too low and whey separates.
x: Vegetables floating above the brine.
Using old yoghurt as starter after day 3.

L.k: A batch that misses its pH limit in time is not used.
p: Salt % on total batch weight (produce + water). Chlorine-free water.
18–22 °C, never above 25 °C. pH with a calibrated meter, not strips.
Reject: coloured fuzzy mould, slime, putrid smell. A flat white film (kahm yeast) is skimmed off.
Jars max 80 % full with a one-way valve. Never a fully tightened lid without a valve.
Vacuum bags: seal at 92–95 % power, bag twice the volume; burp when tight. No inflation by day 3 means fermentation stopped.
Log every batch: salt %, temperature, pH day 0, day 3, final. Keep records 12 months.
x: Strips instead of a pH meter.
Fermenting next to the hot line.

L.k: Salt for texture, acid for flavour. Acid is a finishing tool, not the main process.
p: Marinades act on the surface only.
Near pH 5.0–5.4 (the isoelectric point) muscle protein loses water fast.
Add acid late whenever the dish allows.
When yield matters, skip the acidic marinade.
x: Overnight lemon marinade for fish.
Marinade plus a wet brine together.

quiz: A flat white film on a ferment is:
Critical pH for fermented chilli sauce:

L.k: Size mains by raw protein per guest, multiply by a popularity coefficient K, then add cooking losses.
p: Count every group eating the same buffet before you size anything.
Cooked portion ÷ yield = raw weight (see Yield by cooking method).
K above 1 for favourites (salmon, chicken), below 1 for less popular dishes.
Fewer proteins on the line: each one gets a bigger share per guest and runs out faster.
Raw purchase weights; budget a further 15–25 % cooking loss on proteins.
Salads are the heaviest line by weight and where most waste sits at close.

tb.c: Raw quantity per guest, full spread (4 proteins)

x: Sizing sauce-heavy mains by total dish weight instead of meat per guest.
Forgetting a second group on the same buffet.

L.k: Salt (g) = weight (kg) × g/kg. Use the lower end with cheese, bacon, olives, soy or stock cubes.
p: Percentages are of the finished soup, sauce or salad, or of raw meat as stated.
Taste after acid, then adjust.
Weigh salt for large batches; a pinch does not scale.
x: Salting a salad with feta like a plain one.

L.k: Hot 63 °C +, cold 5 °C or below, small batches, scrambled eggs replaced every 30 min.
p: T −60 min ovens and hot holding on, chillers checked. T −15 min buffet filled, labels and allergen cards in place.
Record hot and cold temperatures every 2 hours.
Never top up a tray: change the whole tray.
At close, discard everything from the buffet except sealed portions.
Live station: ask about allergies first, clean pan for allergy orders.

r: Low heat, stir, off while glossy
Hold in iced water, reheat 30 s
Soft 6 · medium 8 · hard 10 min, then ice
Max 2 h, made fresh each service

x: One full gastronorm sitting for an hour.
Returning buffet leftovers to the fridge.

L.k: Start unstable processes first and never let protein wait. Everything else can.
p: Order of work: long stable processes, prep you can pause, controlled cooking, then à la minute items.
Braises and chilled sous-vide can wait; emulsions only briefly; fish and eggs not at all.
Fix bottlenecks before service: stagger the single pan, batch the fryer, pre-prep complex garnish, cross-train.
Mise en place removes decisions from the moment there is no time to make them.
x: Firing everything at once.
One cook who knows the station.

L.k: Build the plate in eating order. The sauce must hold 3–5 minutes on the way to the table.
p: Sensory order: vision, aroma, first-bite texture, taste, aftertaste.
Every plate needs crisp, tender, creamy and fresh elements.
Fat likes heat, acid likes cold. Never serve every element at the same temperature.
Cold elements go on last.
Every garnish is edible or it does not go on. Negative space tells the eye where to start.

r: Add acid or a cold element

x: Hot acid: reads sharp.
Cold fat-based sauce: muted aroma.

L.k: Choose the fat by heat: tallow and clarified butter for searing, whole butter and EVOO for finishing.
p: Fructose caramelises and burns fastest, sucrose is the most stable.
Pineapple (bromelain) and papaya (papain) enzymes turn meat mushy fast.
Koji tenderises slowly and needs strict control.
Crisp needs dry heat; trapped steam kills it.
x: Deep-frying in extra virgin olive oil.
Pineapple marinade overnight.

quiz: Scrambled eggs on a breakfast buffet are replaced every:
Which process can wait during service?
Cold elements on a plate go on:
The best fat for deep frying:

L.k: Weigh everything critical. Control yield, not purchase price.
p: Selling price = portion cost ÷ target food cost %. Fine dining runs 28–35 %.
Loss happens at trimming (5–20 %), cooking (10–35 %), holding (5–15 %) and reheating (5–10 %).
Standardise trim specs so cost becomes predictable.
Yield tests on fish, lobster and meat: whole → trimmed → cooked; use the % for costing and ordering.
x: Portioning by eye.
Blaming the supplier for a thermal problem.

L.k: Most food-cost problems are thermal problems. A 5 % yield gain is worth an 8–10 % price rise nobody notices.
p: Kitchens make their money in prep: batch size, portioning and regeneration.
Pull steaks early and use carry-over: +5–8 % yield.
Cook and chill sous-vide instead of long hot holding.
Base sauces plus à la minute finish cut labour.
x: Cooking steaks to final temperature in the pan.

L.k: Stock is cash on a shelf. Order from data, rotate always.
p: FIFO for dry and cold stores, FEFO for fresh and high-risk items.
Par levels set minimum stock for stable service.
Count seafood and meat daily, dairy every 2–3 days, dry goods weekly.
Cross-use ingredients across the menu to kill dead stock.
Keep a waste log; trim goes to stocks and staff meals.
x: Ordering by feeling.
Dead stock nobody reports.

L.k: Consistency beats brilliance. Fix the system, not the plate.
p: Prep: weigh salt % and hydration against the written standard.
Cooking: thermometers, not judgement.
Finishing: measured acid and fat.
Plating: portion and photo reference.
Daily reference dish, weekly salt and acid calibration, scheduled team tastings.
Salt changes: chef or sous. Plating or recipe changes: chef only.
x: Recipe drift over months with no written standard.

L.k: Train systems, not personalities. Undocumented knowledge leaves with the person.
p: Junior: prep and hygiene, daily supervision. Line cook: runs a station. Senior: solves problems under pressure. Sous chef: controls the system.
Daily service debrief, weekly skill drills and taste calibration, monthly cross-training.
Measure with timing data, waste logs, re-fires and plating checks.
Promote by competence, not tenure.
x: Shadow-only learning: errors get inherited.

L.k: Calm is control. The team reads the chef before it reads the ticket.
p: Standards are public; if they need interpreting, they are not standards.
Feedback is specific and structured, after service, not shouted across the pass.
Predefined fire order for rushes, cross-training for shortages.
Clear roles stop blame shifting; a career plan stops passive resistance; load balance stops burnout.
x: Emotional reactions during service.
Micromanaging every plate.

quiz: A 5 % yield gain is worth about:

L.k: Dough and butter at the same firmness, cold rests between turns: that is what makes layers.
p: Butter and dough both at about 12–15 °C: the butter bends without cracking or melting.
Rest the dough 30 min in the fridge between turns so the gluten relaxes and the butter firms.
Roll in one direction, brush off flour before folding, keep edges straight.
Bake puff hot, 200–220 °C: steam from the butter lifts the layers.
Croissants proof at 24–27 °C. Warmer and the butter melts out before baking.

r: Rest 30 min after the last roll
Start hot, then lower to finish

x: Skipping rests to save time.
Flour left between layers, which makes them tough.
Proofing croissants near the oven.

L.k: Yolks thicken at 82–84 °C; starch thickens only after a full boil.
p: Crème anglaise: stir to 82–84 °C (coats the spoon), strain, chill fast.
Crème pâtissière: boil 1 minute after it thickens, or the starch stays raw and the cream turns thin.
Crème brûlée: bake in a water bath at 100–150 °C until it wobbles in the centre.
Chantilly: cream at 35 % fat or more, cold, 8–10 % sugar, stop at soft peaks.
Italian meringue and pâte à bombe: syrup at 118–121 °C poured onto whites or yolks.
Raw-egg mousse: pasteurised eggs only. Cool creams below 5 °C, label, use within 48 h.

r: Coats the back of a spoon
Thick and glossy, no starch taste

x: Boiling anglaise: it curdles above 85 °C. Blend at once and strain.
Folding cream into a warm base: the mousse collapses.
Over-whipped cream: grainy, then butter.

L.k: Measure sugar with a probe, never by eye. Temper chocolate by temperature and test it.
p: Wash the pan sides with a wet brush to stop crystals. A little glucose or acid helps.
Seeding method: melt, add 25–30 % chopped tempered chocolate, stir down to working temperature.
Test tempering: a smear on paper sets glossy and snaps within 3–5 min at about 20 °C.
Store chocolate at 15–18 °C, dry and dark. Fat bloom comes from heat, sugar bloom from moisture.
Hot sugar burns deeply: long sleeves, cold water at hand, no distractions.
x: Stirring a syrup after it boils: it crystallises.
Water or steam in melted chocolate: it seizes.
Skipping the test and finding dull, streaky chocolate the next day.

L.k: A good dessert plate has contrast: smooth and crunchy, sweet and sour, warm and cold.
p: Balance sweetness with acid (fruit, yoghurt) and a pinch of salt.
Portion and prep every element before service; only assemble at the pass.
Ice cream is stored at −18 °C and served at −12 to −14 °C: temper the tub before service.
Nut and gluten-free desserts: separate tools, plated first or on a clean station, labelled.
Wipe plate rims, keep height, and serve cold plates for frozen elements.
x: Five sweet elements and no acid.
Ice cream scooped straight from −18 °C: hard and icy.
Garnish that cannot be eaten.

quiz: Ideal butter temperature for lamination is:
Why must crème pâtissière boil for 1 minute?
So the starch thickens fully and the cream stays thick
Italian meringue syrup is cooked to:
Ice cream is best served at:
Fat bloom on chocolate is caused by:

L.k: Every cocktail balances strong, sweet and sour or bitter, plus water from the ice.
p: Always use a jigger: it controls cost, consistency and the alcohol a guest drinks.
Shaking chills and adds about 25 % water; stirring adds about 20 % and keeps the drink clear.
Shake drinks with juice, cream or egg; stir drinks made only of spirits.
Taste with a straw before serving; adjust with drops, not splashes.
Follow local law on measures, age checks and refusing service.

r: Spirit 50 ml : citrus 25 ml : syrup 20–25 ml
Spirit 60 ml : syrup 5–10 ml : 2 dashes bitters

x: Free-pouring.
Old, cloudy ice: it melts fast and waters drinks down.
Juice squeezed yesterday.

L.k: Ice is food: clean scoop, clean bin, and any broken glass means the whole bin is emptied.
p: Simple syrup 1 : 1 sugar to water; rich syrup 2 : 1.
Squeeze citrus for the shift; lime juice changes flavour within hours.
Label syrups and infusions with date; keep them in the fridge.
Never scoop ice with a glass. If a glass breaks near the ice, empty and clean the bin.
Garnish prepped on a clean board, covered, chilled.
x: Ice scooped with a glass.
Unlabelled syrups.
Citrus left in the sun on the bar.

L.k: Espresso is a recipe: dose, yield and time. Tea is temperature and time.
p: Espresso: 7–9 g for a single, 14–18 g for a double; 25–30 s; water 90–96 °C at 9 bar.
Weigh the shot: about twice the dry coffee weight in the cup.
Steam milk to 60–65 °C; hotter tastes cooked and loses sweetness.
Purge the steam wand before and after every jug; backflush the group daily.
Fast shot means grind finer; slow shot means grind coarser.
x: Boiling milk.
Grounds left in the portafilter.
Green tea brewed with boiling water: bitter.

L.k: Match the weight of the drink to the weight of the dish; then use contrast.
p: Acid in the drink cuts fat in the dish.
Tannin softens with protein and fat; it clashes with fish and spicy food.
Dessert wine must be at least as sweet as the dessert.
Spicy food: lower alcohol, a little sweetness.
No-alcohol pairings: shrubs, teas, kombucha and juices with acid and bitterness, not just sugar.

r: Dry sparkling, crisp white, green tea

x: Dry wine with a sweet dessert: the wine tastes sour.
Non-alcoholic menu of sweet juices only.

quiz: Spirit 50 ml : citrus 25 ml : syrup 20–25 ml
Which drinks are stirred rather than shaken?
Glass breaks near the ice bin. You:
Empty and clean the whole bin
Use the ice for cooling bottles only

L.k: Ask, check every component, and keep the answer the same from order to plate.
p: Read the labels of every bought product: stocks, sauces, bread and sweets hide animal products.
Hidden animal products: gelatine, fish sauce, anchovy (Worcestershire), animal rennet in cheese, lard, honey, egg wash.
Halal and kosher are about the source of the meat and how it is handled, not only about pork.
Coeliac guests need gluten-free (under 20 mg/kg) and no cross-contact: clean board, separate fryer and toaster.
Medical diets (diabetic, renal, low-sodium) follow the dietitian's plan; ask, do not guess.

r: Gelatine, fish sauce, animal rennet, meat stock
Honey, butter, egg wash, milk powder
Wine in sauces, gelatine, shared fryers
Flour dust, shared oil, soy sauce, beer

x: Saying yes before checking the stock or sauce.
Vegan dish fried in the same oil as fish.
Taking out the croutons and calling the salad gluten-free.

L.k: Texture is prescribed for the guest by the speech therapist: cook to the level and test every batch.
p: IDDSI is the international standard for texture-modified food and thickened drinks for people with swallowing problems (dysphagia).
Drinks are levels 0–4, foods are levels 3–7. Level 3 and 4 apply to both.
Flow test for drinks: a 10 ml syringe, 10 seconds of flow, then read what is left.
Fork pressure test: press with a fork until the thumbnail blanches. Level 6 food must squash and not spring back.
Spoon tilt test (level 4): the food holds its shape and slides off the spoon in one piece.

r: More than 8 ml left; drips through a fork
No flow; holds shape on a spoon, no lumps
Lumps up to 4 mm (adults), moist, no thin liquid
Pieces up to 1.5 cm (adults), squashes with a fork

x: Mixed textures: soup with bits, cereal in milk, juicy fruit. They are high choking risk.
Dry, crumbly or sticky foods at levels 4–6: bread, rice, nuts, peanut butter.
A garnish of herbs or seeds on a purée.

L.k: Purée each component on its own, shape it, and add back the energy and protein that water takes out.
p: Cook until soft, then blend with its own liquid; pass through a sieve for level 4.
Thicken with the product's thickener at the dose on the label; check again after 5 min, it keeps thickening.
Fortify: cream, butter, milk powder or protein powder, because purée is diluted food.
Moulds and piping make plates look like food; it helps people eat.
Label each container with the IDDSI level, date and allergens; hold hot at 63 °C or cold at 0–4 °C.

r: Braise until tender, blend with sauce, add gelling agent if moulding
Poach, blend with sauce; check for bones before blending
Cook soft, blend, season; set in moulds
Mashed potato is good; rice and pasta must be blended to level
Smooth mousse, custard, purée; no biscuit crumbs or seeds

x: One purée of the whole plate: grey, and you cannot taste anything.
Skipping the test after thickening.
Serving at the wrong level because the ticket was not read.

quiz: Level 6 pieces for adults are up to:
Which is high choking risk at levels 4–6?

L.k: Plan staff from the forecast of covers, not from habit.
p: Start from the forecast: covers, events, deliveries, deep cleans.
Labour cost % = wages ÷ net food sales × 100. Know your target and check it weekly.
Publish the rota early and keep changes rare: it keeps good people.
Know the rest rules where you work. In the EU: 11 h daily rest, 24 h weekly rest, a break on days over 6 h, average 48 h a week maximum.
Cross-train so one sick day does not close a station.
x: Same rota every week whatever the bookings.
Double shifts without rest.
Only one person knows the pastry section.

L.k: Five minutes before service saves an hour of mistakes.
p: Briefing every shift, standing, 5–10 minutes, same order every time.
Cover: covers and timings, VIPs, allergies and diets, specials, 86 list, roles.
Handover is written: what is in progress, fridge temperatures, faults, deliveries, what is low.
End with questions; check that each cook knows their station.
Keep the log: it is your HACCP and training record.

r: Sea bass special; no more lamb
Ana on garnish, Petar on the pass

x: Briefing only when something goes wrong.
Handover by memory.
Allergies not mentioned because "it's on the ticket".

L.k: One voice at the pass: call, confirm, fire, check, send.
p: Every call is answered: "Yes, chef" or "Heard".
Fire by table and by course; time each course from its fire call.
Check every plate: temperature, portion, garnish, rim, allergy flag.
When you fall behind: stop new tables for 2 minutes, reorder tickets, get help, tell front of house.
Track ticket times; review the slow ones after service, not during.

r: Total count of one dish on all tickets

x: Shouting without names.
Sending a plate you would not eat.
Hiding problems from the floor.

L.k: Praise in public, correct in private, and always say what good looks like.
p: Feedback: Situation, Behaviour, Impact, then the next step.
First three days of a new cook: a buddy, written station guide, safety and allergens first.
Check in at 1 week and 1 month: what is clear, what is hard.
Conflict: separate, cool down, listen to both, agree one rule, follow up.
Recognise good work by name. It costs nothing and keeps people.

r: The risotto went out without tasting
Two plates were too salty and came back
Taste every batch; ask me if unsure

x: Correcting people in front of guests or the team.
No training plan for new staff.
Ignoring a conflict until someone leaves.

quiz: A good pre-shift briefing lasts about:
When the kitchen falls behind, first:
Pause new tables briefly, reorder tickets, get help

Sea bass / Sea bream / Trout / Salmon
